title: 1 Kings 16:1–14
context: The prophet Jehu son of Hanani announces that Baasha’s house will share the fate of Jeroboam’s. After Baasha’s death, his son Elah reigns two years until his officer Zimri kills him while he is drunk and destroys Baasha’s family, as the prophet had said. The narrator stresses that judgment follows the LORD’s word. Verse 11 uses a Hebrew idiom for males.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha. Arminian readers note that God sends prophets to kings who have gone astray, a gracious warning that still leaves room for response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign word addressing even the most powerful. Jehu’s father Hanani is likely the seer who rebuked Asa (2 Chronicles 16:7), so a prophetic family confronts kings in both kingdoms.

verses.text: “Because I exalted you out of the dust and made you prince over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have made my people Israel to sin, to provoke me to anger with their sins,
verses.arminianNotes: God says he exalted Baasha from the dust and made him prince, yet Baasha followed Jeroboam. Arminian readers stress that privilege brings responsibility, and that Baasha’s failure was his own response to God’s gift.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God claims to have raised Baasha up, even though Baasha seized the throne by murder. They see God’s rule over who holds power (compare the box at Proverbs 21:1) without excusing the king’s sin.

verses.text: behold, I will utterly sweep away Baasha and his house; and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat.
verses.arminianNotes: God will sweep away Baasha’s house like Jeroboam’s. Arminian readers see judgment that mirrors the king’s own choices, as the destroyer of one house now faces the same fate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the parallel with Jeroboam deliberately drawn. God’s justice is consistent: the same sin brings the same judgment, regardless of who commits it.

verses.text: The dogs will eat Baasha’s descendants who die in the city; and he who dies of his in the field, the birds of the sky will eat.”
verses.arminianNotes: Dogs and birds will eat Baasha’s descendants, the same grim judgment spoken over Jeroboam (14:11). Arminian readers read such language as a severe warning meant to move hearers to repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shame of an unburied death as covenant judgment. The repetition of the curse links the two dynasties as examples of what idolatry brings.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Baasha, and what he did, and his might, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes: Baasha’s other acts and his might are left to the chronicles. Arminian readers note that political strength did not alter God’s verdict on his reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Kings mentions Baasha’s might only in passing. In the narrator’s view, power without faithfulness counts for little. The source citation once again points elsewhere for details the narrator leaves aside.

verses.text: Baasha slept with his fathers, and was buried in Tirzah; and Elah his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Baasha dies and is buried in Tirzah, and Elah succeeds him. Arminian readers note that judgment does not fall immediately, giving his son a further opportunity to turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s timing in the delay: the word against Baasha’s house will be fulfilled in his son’s days, not his own. Judgment is certain even when it is not immediate, a pattern repeated often in Kings.

verses.text: Moreover the LORD’s word came by the prophet Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha and against his house, both because of all the evil that he did in the LORD’s sight, to provoke him to anger with the work of his hands, in being like the house of Jeroboam, and because he struck him.
verses.arminianNotes: The word came against Baasha both for his evil and because he struck Jeroboam’s house. Arminian readers see Baasha held responsible for violence he chose freely, even though it fulfilled a prophecy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Baasha is judged for an act that carried out God’s announced judgment. The existing box at Judges 9:23 discusses how the traditions handle God’s use of evil agents; some interpreters compare Hosea 1:4 on the house of Jehu.

verses.text: In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah the son of Baasha began to reign over Israel in Tirzah for two years.
verses.arminianNotes: Elah begins to reign in Asa’s twenty-sixth year for two years. Arminian readers note the brevity of his reign and the absence of any sign of repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the word spoken against Baasha now hangs over his son. The short reign sets the stage for its fulfillment. His reign begins in Tirzah, where the coming coup will take place.

verses.text: His servant Zimri, captain of half his chariots, conspired against him. Now he was in Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, who was over the household in Tirzah;
verses.arminianNotes: Zimri, a chariot commander, conspires while Elah is drinking himself drunk in a steward’s house. Arminian readers see a king careless of his duties and vulnerable through his own indulgence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elah is drinking while the army besieges Gibbethon (16:15). His negligence becomes the occasion of the judgment God had announced. The steward Arza is named, but the text does not say whether he was involved.

verses.text: and Zimri went in and struck him and killed him in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Zimri kills Elah in Asa’s twenty-seventh year and takes the throne. Arminian readers note the pattern of violence repeating, as one usurper falls to another.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the instability of the northern throne as a recurring sign of judgment. A kingdom built on rebellion is shaken again and again.

verses.text: When he began to reign, as soon as he sat on his throne, he attacked all the house of Baasha. He didn’t leave him a single one who urinates on a wall among his relatives or his friends.
verses.arminianNotes: Zimri destroys Baasha’s house, leaving no male relative or friend. The WEB footnote gives male as an alternate rendering of the idiom. Arminian readers note the ruthless efficiency of political violence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the completeness of the destruction as fulfilling Jehu’s word. Even friends of the house are swept away, showing how thoroughly the dynasty ended.

verses.text: Thus Zimri destroyed all the house of Baasha, according to the LORD’s word which he spoke against Baasha by Jehu the prophet,
verses.arminianNotes: Zimri destroyed Baasha’s house according to the word spoken by Jehu. Arminian readers see the prophetic warning vindicated, though Zimri acted from his own ambition.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that the narrator again ties events to the LORD’s word. History unfolds as God said it would, through the free and sinful acts of men.

verses.text: for all the sins of Baasha, and the sins of Elah his son, which they sinned and with which they made Israel to sin, to provoke the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger with their vanities.
verses.arminianNotes: The reason is the sins of Baasha and Elah, who provoked the LORD with their vanities. Arminian readers stress that judgment follows persistent sin across two generations.
verses.reformedNotes: Vanities is a term for idols as empty and worthless. Reformed readers see the folly of worshiping what has no substance, a theme later prophets develop.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Elah, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Elah’s acts receive only a source citation. Arminian interpreters observe how little of his reign is remembered beyond his failure. His legacy is shaped by the prophetic word spoken against his father’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Elah’s notice is among the shortest, fitting a reign remembered only for drunkenness and death. Even the source citation feels like an epitaph for a dynasty that has ended.
